grammar.intro_en:
Separable phrasal verbs: a noun object can go in the middle or at the end: turn down the music / turn the music down. A pronoun (it, them, him, her) MUST go in the middle: turn it down.
Inseparable phrasal verbs never split: I came across an old photo. I came across it.
grammar.intro_ar: معنى الفعل المركب (phrasal verb) غالبًا لا يُفهم من كلماته منفصلة، فاحفظه كوحدة واحدة مع مثال. أشهر خطأ هو وضع الضمير في آخر الجملة مثل Turn down it أو I looked up it، والصحيح Turn it down و I looked it up. أما الأفعال غير القابلة للفصل فلا نضع شيئًا في وسطها: I'm looking forward to the trip. وانتبه: بعد look forward to يأتي فعل بـ ing لأن to هنا حرف جر: I'm looking forward to seeing you (وليس to see).

rows: object in the middle or at the end
Put off the meeting. / Put the meeting off.
Put it off. (not Put off it)
I came across an old photo. I came across it.
I'm looking forward to the film. We ran out of popcorn.

notes: Separable: put off, turn down / up, look up, pick up, take up, give away, try on, fill in, throw away.
Inseparable: come across, look after, take after, get into, run out of, keep up with, look forward to, get over.
Wrong: I'm looking forward to see you. ✔ I'm looking forward to seeing you.

write_speak: Write & Speak — Write a review (150–200 words) of a book, film, series or concert you enjoyed. Describe it, give your opinion and recommend it. Use at least five phrasal verbs. Then record a one-minute spoken review, as if for your own channel.
other: Example: I recently came across an old copy of Naguib Mahfouz's Palace Walk (Bayn al-Qasrayn) in my father's bookcase, and I couldn't put it down. It is the first part of the famous Cairo Trilogy, and it tells the story of a family living in old Cairo in the years leading up to the 1919 revolution. The father, Al-Sayyid Ahmad Abd al-Jawad, is strict and serious at home but fun-loving with his friends outside. His wife, Amina, spends her life looking after the family and almost never leaves the house. Their children grow up in a changing country, and their dreams and problems are very moving. The plot is slow at the beginning, so some readers might give up after a few chapters. My advice is: don't! Once you get into the story, it becomes gripping. I had to look up a few historical events, but that made it even more interesting. In my opinion, the novel is not overrated at all. Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988, and after reading this book, I understand why. I'm already looking forward to reading the second part, Palace of Desire. A must-read!
